opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it was partly practical and partly a question of what I thought the real bottleneck was.

When I joined the lab, there was this wheelchair-mounted robot arm project, a feeding-assistance kind of setup. The motivation was beautiful: help people with limited mobility eat on their own. But once I started working on it, I kept running into the same wall. The hard part wasn't the wheelchair or the overall system. It was the manipulation itself, picking up a piece of food reliably, with precision, without crushing it or dropping it. The full system had so many moving parts, perception, the user interface, safety, the arm mounting, that it was hard to isolate and really study that core problem.

So I asked myself: what's the simplest possible tool that still captures what makes fine manipulation hard? And chopsticks came to mind, partly because I grew up using them. They're just two sticks, but humans can pick up a peanut, a noodle, a slippery piece of tofu. All the dexterity lives in how you control them, not in some complicated hardware. That felt like the perfect testbed: cheap, easy to build, easy to fix when it breaks, and it forces you to confront precision and control directly.

There was also a very selfish, grad-student reason. When you build your own small robot, you own the whole loop. I could iterate fast, break things, rebuild them in a day, collect data whenever I wanted. With a big shared platform, every change involves coordination and risk. For learning how to do research, having something small that I fully understood was incredibly valuable.

And in a way, it wasn't really leaving the feeding project behind. If you can make a robot use chopsticks well, that skill transfers back to things like assistive feeding. I just felt I had to go one level deeper first.

r001.rationale: The response says the wheelchair project’s many components made manipulation hard to isolate, but it does not identify a mismatch with the machine-learning work Kay wanted to pursue.

r002.rationale: The response deliberately chooses chopsticks as a testbed because they require difficult, precise manipulation and control.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it wasn't a dramatic decision. The wheelchair project was a good project, a mature one, with a lot of people already on it. But there's a problem with a mature project: by the time you join, most of the interesting questions have already been answered. You end up tuning parameters someone else chose, fixing edge cases in a system you didn't design. That's valuable work, and someone has to do it, but I was at a point where I needed to understand the whole stack myself, from the first line of code to the last screw.

The chopsticks idea came from something very small. I was eating lunch and watching my own hand, and I realized how absurd the task is. Two sticks, no joints between them, no suction, no gripper. All the intelligence lives in the fingers and in the perception. You can't cheat with a clever end effector, because the end effector is deliberately stupid. So the robot has to be good at the parts that are actually hard: contact, friction, slipping, recovering when the dumpling starts to roll away. Those are exactly the problems I thought were underexplored, and they show up everywhere, not just at the dinner table.

The other reason is scale. A wheelchair is big, expensive, and if something goes wrong there's a person sitting in it. A chopsticks arm fits on a desk. I could break it ten times a day and nobody gets hurt. When you're learning, the speed of iteration matters more than the prestige of the project. I'd rather fail fast on something small and honest than succeed slowly on something where I only owned a corner of it.

And I'll admit there's an element of taste. The wheelchair solves a problem for someone else. The chopsticks solved a curiosity for me. In the long run I think you build better things when you start from the thing you can't stop thinking about.

r002.rationale: The response explains that Kay chose chopstick manipulation because it presents difficult, underexplored challenges such as contact, friction, slipping, and recovery.

astra-6.text: I wanted a project I could take from an idea to a working prototype myself. With the wheelchair robot, I would have been contributing to something that already had a direction. The chopsticks robot gave me a smaller, concrete problem to explore: could I make a robot pick up food using a tool we use every day? It sounds simple, but it brings together a lot of interesting challenges—movement, grip, and handling different kinds of food. That made it feel like a good project to learn by building.

With the existing wheelchair robot, I would have been contributing to something whose direction was already established. Building a chopsticks robot gave me a chance to define the problem myself and work through the design decisions. It also appealed to me because eating with chopsticks is such an ordinary action for a person, but getting a robot to do it raises some interesting challenges.
